blocks.text: Visual question answering, VQA, fine-tuning trains a model to answer a specific natural language question about an image, extending the vision-language model foundations covered in an earlier topic of this module into a more targeted, question-driven task than the open-ended image captioning covered in the previous topic.

This topic covers how VQA differs from captioning, the open-ended versus closed-set answer distinction, and why counting, spatial, and reasoning questions each present their own specific difficulty for a fine-tuned VQA model.

VQA fine-tuning teaches a model to take both an image and a natural language question about that image as input, and produce a correct answer, building on the same vision-language model foundation, covered in an earlier topic, that underlies the other multimodal tasks in this module.

Image captioning, covered in the previous topic, produces a general description of an image without any specific question guiding what to focus on, VQA instead answers a specific, targeted question, requiring the model to focus on exactly the part of the image the question concerns rather than describing everything present.

A VQA model architecture typically encodes the image and the question separately, then fuses these representations together so the model can reason jointly about visual content and the specific question being asked, before producing an answer grounded in both.

Some VQA training setups treat the task as open-ended generation, producing a free text answer, others constrain it to a closed set, yes or no questions, or a fixed list of possible answers, closed-set framing simplifies both training and evaluation but cannot handle questions whose correct answer falls outside the predefined set.

blocks.text: Counting questions, "how many chairs," require the model to enumerate distinct objects accurately, spatial questions, "what is left of the table," require understanding relative position, and reasoning questions, "is it raining," require inferring information not directly labeled in the image, each of these question categories benefits from dedicated representation in training data since they stress different model capabilities.

blocks.title: Counting is a persistently hard category for VQA models
blocks.content: Even strong vision-language models frequently make counting errors, especially with larger numbers of objects or partially occluded items, a known weak point worth specifically testing during evaluation.

blocks.text: Simple exact match scoring, covered generally in an earlier topic, undercounts genuinely correct answers phrased differently, VQA evaluation commonly instead uses a human consensus approach, collecting multiple human answers per question and scoring a model answer as correct if it matches enough of that consensus, accounting for legitimate answer variation.

Some images genuinely support more than one reasonable answer to the same question, an object partially out of frame or an ambiguous color under unusual lighting, training and evaluation data that acknowledges this ambiguity, rather than forcing a single ground truth answer, produces a more realistic and fair evaluation.

VQA training data is typically collected by showing annotators images and having them write both questions and answers, or by having a separate set of annotators answer pre-written questions, with multiple independent answers per question supporting the consensus evaluation approach covered above.

VQA fine-tuning commonly supports accessibility tools answering questions about images for visually impaired users, visual product search where users ask questions about a photographed item, and automated visual inspection systems answering specific questions about captured images.

A team building an accessibility tool fine-tunes a VQA model to answer open-ended questions users ask about photos they take, initial evaluation using strict exact match scoring shows disappointing results despite the answers looking reasonable on manual review.

Switching to a human consensus evaluation approach, collecting several valid phrasings per question from human annotators, reveals the model was actually performing much better than exact match suggested, most failures were phrasing differences rather than genuine errors, with the remaining real errors concentrated specifically in counting questions, prompting a targeted data augmentation effort for that question category.

items: Evaluating VQA with strict exact match scoring, undercounting correct answers phrased differently
Underrepresenting counting and spatial reasoning questions in training data, leaving known weak categories untested
Forcing a single ground truth answer onto genuinely ambiguous questions rather than accounting for valid variation
Confusing VQA with image captioning, when the two tasks require fundamentally different attention to the question itself

blocks.text: Pick an image you are familiar with and write three questions about it, one counting question, one spatial question, and one reasoning question, then consider what specific visual understanding each question type would require a VQA model to demonstrate correctly.

Visual question answering fine-tunes a model to answer specific natural language questions about an image by fusing image and question representations, distinct from the general description task of image captioning covered in the previous topic, with counting, spatial, and reasoning questions each presenting their own difficulty, and reliable evaluation needing a human consensus approach rather than strict exact match to fairly account for valid answer variation.
